books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, A. Migrations and New Communities in the Age of the Market Revolution

primary_sources: John L. O'Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity” (1839)

stimulus.text: John L. O’Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, November 1839: “American patriotism is not of soil; we are not aborigines, nor of ancestry, for we are of all nations; but it is essentially personal enfranchisement, for ‘where liberty dwells,’ said Franklin, the sage of the Revolution, ‘there is my country.’” O’Sullivan also wrote that “the nation of many nations is destined to manifest to mankind the excellence of divine principles.”
stimulus.source_note: John L. O'Sullivan, “The Great Nation of Futurity,” United States Magazine and Democratic Review, vol. 6, no. 23 (November 1839), pp. 426-430. Verbatim quotations verified against Wikisource. Survivor rewrite of pr25e-test1-q18: new stimulus passage, new stem, new options, new explanations.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: O'Sullivan's celebration of a nation “of all nations” sits uneasily with which development of the same period?

options.text: The growth of canals linking the East and the West
options.misconception: Canals tied regions together; they did not contradict O'Sullivan's praise of a nation of many nations.

options.text: The spread of the telegraph across the country
options.misconception: The telegraph spread news; it has nothing to do with who counts as American.

options.text: The rise of textile mills in New England
options.misconception: The mills hired immigrants and farm daughters; they do not clash with O'Sullivan's claim the way removal does.

options.text: The forced removal of Native peoples in the East

rationales.A: Canals moved goods and people across the country. They fit O'Sullivan's picture of a growing nation; they do not contradict it.
rationales.B: The telegraph is about communication, not about membership in the nation. It sits beside his claim, not against it.
rationales.C: Mill towns were full of immigrants, the very people O'Sullivan celebrates. The mills do not expose a limit in his welcome.
rationales.D: O'Sullivan writes “we are not aborigines,” leaving Native peoples out of his nation of many nations. In the same decades, the United States forced Native peoples off their eastern lands, so his welcome did not extend to them.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who his welcome covers. Immigrants from many nations, bound by liberty.
2. Ask who it leaves out. He writes “we are not aborigines.”
3. Match the exclusion to a policy. Removal forced Native peoples off their lands in the East.
Background: The Removal Act of 1830 authorized moving tribes west of the Mississippi, and the Cherokee were forced out in 1838.
Remember: a welcome that names who belongs also names who does not, so read the exclusion.
